I am 62 years old, and I have farmed my land in Quzhou County since I was a young man. My father taught me, and his father taught him. I only finished primary school, but I know this soil and this climate better than any book.

This spring, my winter wheat that I sowed last October on my five mu is already turning green after the cold months. I will not abandon it for anything new — wheat and maize in rotation is what this land was made for, and it is what feeds my family. Everyone around here does the same. I have seen too many neighbors try fancy crops and lose money. I stick with what works.

For my wheat, I will rotary-till before sowing — I always do. I use improved wheat seeds, about 30 jin per mu. I spread compound fertilizer as basal before sowing, and I will topdress with urea when the wheat starts jointing in spring. Water is precious, so I irrigate three times: once when the wheat wakes up, once at jointing, and once at heading. That is enough. I spray for insects twice, use herbicide once, and fungicide once when the weather turns damp. I expect about 1000 jin per mu — sometimes a bit more, sometimes less, depending on the rain.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will plant summer maize immediately on the same five mu. There is no time to waste — the frost comes in October. I buy hybrid maize seed from the shop every year, one small package per mu, because hybrid seed gives good yield but you cannot save it. I plant it no-tillage, right into the wheat stubble. I put down compound fertilizer at sowing. The maize needs two irrigations in summer — one when it is knee-high, one at flowering. I spray for insects twice and herbicide once. No fungicide — maize here is strong. I expect about 1100 jin per mu if the summer storms do not flood it.

This is my plan. It is the same plan I have used for decades, and it has never failed to put food on the table.
